title: Sand and varnish wooden furniture
intro: Tired bedside table or stool? Sand it back and give it two fresh coats of varnish.

steps.t: Remove knobs and hardware and stand the piece on newspaper in a well-ventilated room.
Sand everything with grit 120, always along the grain, until the old finish is dull and even.
Go over it with grit 180, then 240, along the grain, until it feels smooth.
steps.q: Is the surface smooth and evenly dull, with no shiny patches?
steps.fix: Go back over the shiny patches with grit 120, then 180 and 240 again.

steps.t: Vacuum the dust, then wipe with a tack cloth or a barely damp cloth until it comes away clean.
Stir the varnish, don't shake it, and brush on a thin coat along the grain in long strokes.
steps.w: Keep a window open, no flames nearby, and read the safety label on the tin.

steps.t: Let it dry, usually about 4 hours: check the time on the tin.
steps.label: Drying

steps.t: Sand lightly with grit 240 until the raised fibres are gone, then dust off.
steps.q: Is it smooth without sanding through to bare wood?
steps.fix: If you went through, dab a thin touch-up coat on that spot and let it dry before the second coat.

steps.t: Brush on the second thin coat the same way, without going back over areas already drying.
Let it harden for 24 hours before using it or refitting the knobs.
steps.label: Hardening

tips: Want a new colour? Apply wood stain first, let it dry as the tin says, then varnish over it.
Thick old paint or varnish? Start with grit 80, or use a paint stripper.
Wrap the brush in cling film between coats so it doesn't dry out.

title: Fix a wobbly wooden chair
intro: Wooden chair rocking? Reglue the loose joint and it'll be solid again.

steps.t: Turn the chair upside down on a blanket and wiggle each leg and rail: find the joint that moves.
steps.q: Have you found the joint that moves?
steps.fix: Sit on it and rock gently while someone watches: an open joint shows a thin dark line or a gap.

steps.t: If there are screws or corner blocks under the seat, tighten them first: sometimes that's all it needs.
Tap the loose joint apart with the rubber mallet, a cloth in between; leave the firm joints alone.
Scrape the old glue off the tenon and out of the hole with the chisel, down to clean wood.
steps.w: Always scrape with the chisel moving away from the hand holding the piece.

steps.t: Dry-fit: push the joint back together without glue.
steps.q: Does the dry joint fit snugly, with no play?
steps.fix: If it's loose, glue a thin wood shaving onto the tenon, or wrap it in thin cotton cloth soaked in glue.

steps.t: Spread a thin coat of wood glue on the tenon and inside the hole.
Push the joint home, tap it with the mallet until it's closed and wipe off squeeze-out with the damp cloth.
Wrap the strap around the legs at the height of the joint and tighten until the joint closes.
Stand the chair on a flat floor and look at all four legs.
steps.q: Do all four legs touch the floor?
steps.fix: Loosen the strap, press the high corner down and retighten before the glue grabs.

steps.t: Leave the strap on and don't sit on it for 24 hours, or as long as the glue says.
steps.label: Glue curing

steps.t: Take the strap off and pare away any dried glue drips with the chisel.

tips: Joint won't come apart? Drill a [[2 mm]] hole in a hidden spot and inject glue with a syringe.
A car ratchet strap works as a band clamp: slip cardboard under it to protect the wood.
If a leg or the seat is cracked, not just loose, take it to a joiner.
